definition: A chunk of text (roughly 3-4 characters in English) that a language model reads and writes. Context windows are measured in tokens; 128k tokens is about 90000 words.
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once when generating a response. Larger windows let the model use more retrieved chunks in RAG.
The neural network architecture behind modern LLMs, introduced in 2017. Its core innovation is the attention mechanism.
The mechanism that lets a model weigh which earlier tokens matter most when predicting the next token, e.g. linking 'it' back to 'animal' instead of 'street'.
Training a model on trillions of tokens from the web and books so it learns grammar, facts and reasoning patterns from next-token prediction.
Further training a pretrained model on curated examples to specialize it, e.g. instruction tuning teaches it to follow user instructions.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: aligning model behavior with human preferences using ranked human feedback on model outputs.
When a model generates plausible-sounding but false text. It happens because the model predicts likely continuations, not verified truth.
A list of numbers (a vector) representing the meaning of text. Similar meanings produce similar vectors, enabling semantic search.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors, used to compare embeddings. Near 1.0 means very similar meaning; it ignores vector magnitude.
The geometric space where embeddings live. Documents and queries must use the same embedding model or their vector spaces won't align.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: connecting an LLM to your own documents. The model retrieves relevant passages first, then generates an answer grounded in them.
Splitting documents into smaller pieces before embedding. Good starting range is 300-800 tokens with 10-20 percent overlap on semantic boundaries.
The number of most similar chunks retrieved for a question. Higher k improves recall but risks exceeding the context window.
Combining keyword search (BM25) with vector search to catch both exact terms and semantic matches, fixing retrieval misses.
A second, more precise model that re-orders retrieved chunks so only the best few fill the limited context window.
Like a table in a relational database. Holds points sharing the same vector size and distance metric, one per use case.
A single record in Qdrant with an id, a vector (the embedding), and a payload of metadata such as source filename and text.
JSON metadata attached to a point. Searches can filter on payload fields, e.g. only documents from a specific source.
Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a graph index for approximate nearest-neighbor search, logarithmic instead of scanning every vector.
How vector similarity is measured. Options include Cosine, Dot product, Euclidean and Manhattan; Cosine is most common for text.
The instruction that sets the model's role and ground rules before the user message, e.g. answer ONLY from provided context.
Including input-output examples in the prompt so the model imitates the pattern, improving format consistency like citations.
Controls randomness: 0.0-0.3 for deterministic factual answers, 0.8-1.2 for creative tasks like brainstorming.
Asking the model to perform a task with no examples, relying only on the instruction itself.
When a model invokes functions described with a JSON schema. Your code executes the function and returns the result to the conversation.
Reason + Act: the agent loop of Thought, Action, Observation repeated until the task is done.
Model Context Protocol: a standard for exposing tools to AI agents so any compliant client can discover and call them.
An agent pattern that decomposes a goal into sub-tasks first, then works through them, replanning when something fails.
The share of test questions where the correct chunk appears in the top-k retrieved results. Cheap, deterministic, catches most RAG regressions.
Whether every claim in the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context, often scored by an LLM judge.
Whether the [1], [2] markers in an answer point at chunks that actually contain the cited claim.
The known-correct document chunk for a test question, used to score whether retrieval found it.
A fixed set of test questions run on every change to prompts, chunking, models or retrieval, tracked over time like a test suite.
